clue.text: He takes things as he finds them

definitions.text: He takes things as he finds them

parts.words: He takes things as he finds them
parts.note: reads like someone easy-going who accepts life as it comes, but describes a compulsive thief who pockets whatever he comes across

explanation.surface: A placid man who accepts whatever comes his way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes things as he finds them' is an idiom for being easy-going; read literally it means picking up and pocketing whatever he finds.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with a compulsive urge to steal helps himself to whatever objects he happens upon.

clue.text: See punk excited in lively party

indicators.note: excited suggests the letters of the two words are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: Watch the agitated punk rocker at a raucous party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' turns SEE and PUNK into the letters of the answer. A KNEES-UP is British slang for a boisterous party with dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A boisterous British celebration with dancing and singing is a lively party.

clue.text: Pier has head removed for the painter

indicators.note: losing its head means the first letter of the pier word is dropped

parts.note: a jetty is a pier or landing stage

explanation.surface: A pier is beheaded for the sake of an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has head removed' drops the J from JETTY. William Etty was an English painter known for nudes.
explanation.definitionFit: William Etty was a nineteenth-century English artist, so he is a painter.

clue.text: Treatment of those people admitting blame?

indicators.note: admitting means letting something in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: they is the pronoun for those people
to take the rap is to take the blame

explanation.surface: Is therapy for people who confess their faults?
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitting' means letting in, so one word takes the other inside; 'take the rap' is the idiom for accepting blame.
explanation.definitionFit: Therapy is a course of medical or psychological care, a form of treatment.

clue.text: British Summer Time in Rome, perhaps, or Clyde for example

indicators.note: in places the time abbreviation inside the rearranged city letters
perhaps signals that Rome is only one possible arrangement of its letters

parts.note: the letters of the city name are used as fodder
BST is the standard abbreviation for British Summer Time

explanation.surface: Summer time in Rome or Scotland's River Clyde, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' says Rome is one possible arrangement, and 'in' puts the time abbreviation inside. Clyde Barrow, of Bonnie and Clyde, was a 1930s American gangster.
explanation.definitionFit: Clyde Barrow was a notorious American gangster, an example of a criminal hoodlum.

clue.text: Where to keep savings account for a house?

definitions.text: Where to keep savings account for a house?

parts.words: Where to keep savings account for a house?
parts.note: reads as banking advice about a home deposit, but points to the place where a saver's egg is kept and where a bird makes its home

explanation.surface: Advice on which savings account to use when buying a home.
explanation.walkthrough: Money put by is called an 'egg' kept in this place, and a bird builds one as its house.
explanation.definitionFit: Savings set aside are pictured as an egg kept in a bird's home of twigs, which is also that bird's house.

clue.text: Vitamin B for former Minister of Health?

explanation.surface: A vitamin supplement for an ex-health secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: Aneurin Bevan was the British Minister of Health who founded the National Health Service in 1948.
explanation.definitionFit: Thiamine, vitamin B1, was once called aneurin, and Bevan, the Labour politician who launched the NHS, bore that first name.

clue.text: Violinist, first in place, is going backwards in the main

parts.note: Isaac Stern was a celebrated violinist
foremost means first in position

explanation.surface: A leading violinist goes into reverse at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea; a ship moving backwards goes with its rear end leading.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel moving in reverse on the ocean travels with its back end leading.

clue.text: Whom to see with Pat's rheumatic prescription?

indicators.note: a prescription is made up by a chemist, hinting that the letters are mixed into a fresh order

parts.note: the letters of Pat's, including the s

explanation.surface: Who to visit with a prescription for Pat's rheumatism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prescription' signals the rearrangement of PATS and RHEUMATIC; the person you take a prescription to is the one who dispenses drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemist who dispenses drugs is the person to visit to have a doctor's prescription made up.

clue.text: Support for Lester coming unstuck after first at Towcester

indicators.note: after puts the rearranged name behind the single letter
first at picks the opening letter of the racecourse name
coming unstuck suggests the name falls apart and is reassembled

explanation.surface: A jockey named Lester comes a cropper at a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first at' picks the opening letter of Towcester, an English racecourse; 'coming unstuck' rearranges the jockey's name, which goes 'after' that letter. The surface evokes jockey Lester Piggott.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is a framework of legs that holds up a table top, so it is a support.

clue.text: Make strong request for British cheese-spread

indicators.note: spread suggests the letters are scattered and laid out anew

explanation.surface: Asking for a British spreadable cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like part of a food phrase, cheese spread, but signals the rearrangement of the cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: To implore someone is to ask them urgently, making a strong request.

clue.text: Impetuous outbreak

explanation.surface: A sudden eruption of hasty action.
explanation.definitionFit: A reckless person acts without thinking, and spots breaking out on the skin are also this word.

clue.text: Starchy food for Dad's Army

parts.note: pa is dad, so Dad's gives pa's
TA is the Territorial Army, the British volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: Food supplies for the Home Guard of Dad's Army.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a British TV sitcom about the wartime Home Guard; the Territorial Army is Britain's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaroni and spaghetti are dough products full of carbohydrate, a starchy food.

clue.text: Uncle Remus's brother?

parts.note: reads as a question about a relative, but asks for the title used before animal names in the Uncle Remus folk tales

explanation.surface: Asking about the sibling of the storyteller Uncle Remus.
explanation.walkthrough: In Joel Chandler Harris's Uncle Remus stories the animals are called Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox and so on, the dialect form of a sibling title.
explanation.definitionFit: In the dialect of those Southern folk tales, the word is the form of address meaning a male sibling.

clue.text: He appears in Some Like it Hot"

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A man has a part in the film Some Like It Hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes some of 'Like it Hot', the 1959 Billy Wilder comedy, whose title the surface quotes.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name stands for a male person, the 'he' who turns up in the title.

clue.text: Die for something from the catalogue?

explanation.surface: A death foretold by an item in a mail-order list.
explanation.definitionFit: A die is a tool for impressing a design, as this device is, and philatelists choose items from a catalogue of postage labels.

clue.text: It's vain foolishness to rewrite Fry and Pope

indicators.note: to rewrite suggests the two names are written out again in a different order

explanation.surface: It is futile to edit the poets Christopher Fry and Alexander Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to rewrite' rearranges FRY and POPE; Fry and Pope were English poets.
explanation.definitionFit: A dandy's vanity in dress and manners is silly conceit, a vain foolishness.

clue.text: No corner-house, this

parts.note: reads as a remark about a building not on a street corner, but describes a round building that has no corners at all

explanation.surface: A remark that this house does not stand on a street corner.
explanation.walkthrough: A corner house is one at a street junction; a round building has no corners anywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular domed building has curved walls, so it has no angles.

clue.text: Hot-rod driver?

parts.note: reads as someone racing a souped-up car, but describes a worker hammering red-hot metal pins into place

explanation.surface: Who drives a souped-up car?
explanation.walkthrough: Shipyard workers drove red-hot metal pins through plates and hammered them flat.
explanation.definitionFit: A metalworker who fastens plates with heated bolts drives those glowing pins home.

clue.text: Virginia with donation for tramp

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for the US state of Virginia
a grant is a donation of money

explanation.surface: Virginia gives money to a homeless wanderer.
explanation.definitionFit: A homeless wanderer with no fixed abode is a tramp.

clue.text: Does he keep cats eyes to himself?

definitions.text: Does he keep cats eyes to himself?

parts.words: Does he keep cats eyes to himself?
parts.note: reads as a question about someone hoarding feline eyes, but describes a driver who stays astride the reflective studs down the middle of the road

explanation.surface: Asking whether a man keeps a cat's eyes for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Cat's eyes are the reflective studs set along the centre line of British roads; a selfish motorist straddles them, hogging the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A selfish motorist who drives down the middle and blocks others hogs the highway.

clue.text: Eastern beast on its back, showing plates

indicators.note: on its back means the words are turned upside down, read backwards in an across light

parts.note: an animal is a beast

explanation.surface: An oriental creature lying on its back, displaying armour plates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on its back' turns E plus ANIMAL right round.
explanation.definitionFit: Laminae are thin layers or scales, such as plates of bone or rock.

clue.text: Graphite without lead produces painful complaint

indicators.note: without lead means the leading letter is dropped

parts.note: plumbago is another name for graphite

explanation.surface: Pencil graphite, minus its lead, causes a painful ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without lead' drops the P of PLUMBAGO, an old name for graphite; the pencil 'lead' surface misleads, as pencil lead is graphite.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumbago is pain in the lower back, a painful complaint.

clue.text: I, in converted van, take summer abroad — for the greenness, say

indicators.note: in puts the I inside the rearranged van letters
converted suggests the van is altered into a different arrangement

parts.note: the three letters of van are used
ete is French for summer

explanation.surface: A traveller in a converted van spends summer overseas, which sounds green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' rearranges the van, 'in' puts I inside it, and 'take' joins the French word for summer, signalled by 'abroad'.
explanation.definitionFit: Naivety is innocent inexperience, the inexperience called greenness.

clue.text: Cruelly attacks big pots

explanation.surface: Someone violently attacks large cups.
explanation.definitionFit: To rob someone violently in the street is to waylay them, and large drinking cups with handles are also this word.

clue.text: Bandleader with troops is mentally unsound

parts.note: the first letter of the word band
an army is a body of troops

explanation.surface: A bandleader with a regiment has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bandleader' reads as a conductor but gives B, the letter leading 'band'.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is British slang for crazy, mentally unsound.

clue.text: Suspicion of a wrinkle, perhaps

explanation.surface: A faint doubt about a crease in the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'wrinkle' is old slang for a useful tip or trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A trace or suggestion of something is a slight suspicion, and a handy tip is called a wrinkle.

clue.text: Repeated note from La Boheme"

indicators.note: repeated means the note is given twice in a row

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A recurring note in Puccini's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Mimi is the heroine of Puccini's opera La Boheme.
explanation.definitionFit: The seamstress who dies of consumption is the heroine character of Puccini's opera.

clue.text: River sport

explanation.surface: A water sport on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wear is a river in north-east England; to sport a tie is to wear it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wear flows through Durham, and to sport clothes is to have them on.

clue.text: Sash-pin arranged the Castilian way

indicators.note: arranged suggests the letters are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A sash pinned the Castilian way.
explanation.definitionFit: Castilian is the standard language of Spain, so the Castilian way is the Spanish way.

clue.text: Eternal sea-legs trouble

indicators.note: trouble suggests the letters are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: A never-ending struggle to find one's balance on board ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges SEALEGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that never grows old is timeless, eternal.

clue.text: Architect's continuous moulding of spaghetti, say?

explanation.surface: An architect's moulding made from pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: In architecture a string course is a horizontal band of stone along a wall; spaghetti is a string-shaped dish served as one course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A horizontal projecting band on a building facade, and a dish of long thin pasta served as part of a meal.
